## Proof

**Claim:** Yes, $x_n \to x$.

**Proof by contradiction.** Suppose $x_n \not\to x$. Then there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ and a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ such that

$$|x_{n_k} - x| \ge \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } k.$$

Define $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by

$$f(t) = \max\!\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{|t - x|}{\varepsilon}\right).$$

This $f$ is continuous (it is the maximum of two continuous functions) and bounded ($0 \le f(t) \le 1$ for all $t$).

Evaluating at $x$:

$$f(x) = \max(0,\; 1 - 0) = 1.$$

Evaluating along the subsequence, since $|x_{n_k} - x| \ge \varepsilon$:

$$\frac{|x_{n_k} - x|}{\varepsilon} \ge 1 \implies 1 - \frac{|x_{n_k} - x|}{\varepsilon} \le 0 \implies f(x_{n_k}) = 0 \quad \text{for all } k.$$

Thus $f(x_{n_k}) \to 0$, while $f(x) = 1$. A subsequence of $(f(x_n))_{n\ge1}$ converges to $0 \ne 1 = f(x)$, so the full sequence $(f(x_n))$ cannot converge to $f(x)$.

This contradicts the hypothesis that $f(x_n) \to f(x)$ for every bounded continuous $f$. Therefore the assumption $x_n \not\to x$ is false, and we conclude

$$x_n \to x. \qquad \blacksquare$$
